name: Paul
title: Apostle to the Gentiles
tagline: Persecutor of the church, called on the road to Damascus.
story: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who persecuted the church until the risen Jesus met him near Damascus; as Paul he carried the gospel to the Gentiles.

periods.title: The church in Acts
periods.sub: Three journeys, arrest, Rome; the letters

periods.title: After Scripture
periods.sub: Tradition, by who said it and when

entries.title: Born at Tarsus, brought up in Jerusalem
entries.text: Born a Jew in Tarsus in Cilicia, “a citizen of no mean city”, and “brought up in this city” (Jerusalem) “at the feet of Gamaliel”.

entries.title: A tentmaker
entries.text: A tentmaker, who worked with his own hands to keep himself and those with him.

entries.title: Of the tribe of Benjamin
entries.text: An Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin, “Circumcised the eighth day”, “an Hebrew of the Hebrews”.

entries.title: A Pharisee, son of a Pharisee
A Roman citizen from birth
entries.text: A Roman citizen from birth: “But I was free born.”

entries.title: His sister’s son
entries.text: His sister's son in Jerusalem warned him of a plot to kill him.

entries.title: “My kinsmen”
entries.text: He calls Andronicus and Junia, Herodion, and Lucius, Jason and Sosipater “my kinsmen”.

entries.title: At Stephen’s stoning
entries.text: A “young man … whose name was Saul” kept the clothes of those who stoned Stephen, and “was consenting unto his death”.

entries.title: Making havock of the church
entries.text: He “made havock of the church”, putting men and women in prison, and asked the high priest for letters to bring believers bound from Damascus.

entries.title: Seen by the risen Lord “last of all”
Damascus, Arabia, the basket
entries.text: After his conversion he preached in the synagogues of Damascus, went into Arabia, came back to Damascus, and escaped over the wall in a basket.

entries.title: Fifteen days with Peter
entries.text: “After three years” he went up to Jerusalem to see Peter and stayed fifteen days; Barnabas brought him to the apostles. He was then sent to Tarsus and worked in “the regions of Syria and Cilicia”.

entries.title: A trance in the temple: “Depart: for I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles”
A year at Antioch
entries.text: Barnabas brought him to Antioch, where they taught for a whole year, and the two carried famine relief to Jerusalem.

entries.title: The first journey
entries.text: First journey: sent out from Antioch with Barnabas to Cyprus and the cities of Pisidia and Lycaonia; at Lystra he was stoned and left for dead.

entries.title: The council at Jerusalem
entries.text: At the council in Jerusalem he and Barnabas told what God had done among the Gentiles.

entries.title: The second journey
entries.text: He parted from Barnabas over Mark and set out with Silas. Timothy joined them at Lystra; a vision called them to Macedonia; they went on to Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea and Athens, and he stayed eighteen months at Corinth.

entries.title: A vision at Corinth: “Be not afraid, but speak”
Three years at Ephesus
entries.text: Third journey: “by the space of three years” he worked from Ephesus, then went through Macedonia and Greece and said farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus.

entries.title: Seized, held, heard
entries.text: Seized in the temple at Jerusalem, he was held two years at Caesarea under Felix; before Festus he appealed to Caesar, and he spoke before King Agrippa.

entries.title: At night in Jerusalem: “so must thou bear witness also at Rome”
Shipwreck, and Rome
entries.text: On the voyage to Rome the ship was wrecked at Melita (Malta). At Rome he lived two whole years in his own hired house with a soldier guarding him, receiving all who came.

entries.title: His own list of sufferings
entries.text: His own list of sufferings: five times thirty-nine lashes, three beatings with rods, one stoning, three shipwrecks, “in prisons more frequent”.

entries.title: The prisons
entries.text: Prisons named in Scripture: Philippi, where he and Silas were put in the stocks; Herod's judgment hall at Caesarea; and Rome. In several letters he writes as a prisoner.

entries.title: Plans for Spain
entries.text: He planned to go on from Rome to Spain.

entries.title: Journeys in the letters
entries.text: The letters to Timothy and Titus name journeys that are hard to place in Acts: Timothy left at Ephesus when Paul went into Macedonia, Titus left in Crete, a winter planned at Nicopolis, a cloak left at Troas and Trophimus left sick at Miletum.

entries.title: Clement of Rome, 1 Clement 5:5-7
entries.text: Clement of Rome writes that Paul had been “seven times in bonds”, had “preached in the East and in the West”, reached “the farthest bounds of the West”, and when he had borne his testimony before the rulers “departed from the world”.

entries.title: Dionysius of Corinth, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 2.25.8
entries.text: Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, writes that Peter and Paul taught in Italy and “suffered martyrdom at the same time”.
entries.who: Dionysius of Corinth, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 2.25.8
entries.when: Dionysius about AD 170; Eusebius about AD 325

entries.title: The Muratorian fragment
entries.text: The Muratorian fragment says Luke's Acts leaves out “the journey of Paul, when he went from the city—Rome—to Spain”.
entries.when: the writer is placed in the latter half of the 2nd century

entries.title: Tertullian, The Prescription Against Heretics 36
entries.text: Tertullian writes that at Rome “Paul wins his crown in a death like John's”: the Baptist's, that is, by beheading.

entries.title: Gaius, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 2.25.7
entries.text: Gaius, a Roman churchman, points to the apostles' “trophies” at the Vatican and on the Ostian Way.
entries.who: Gaius, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 2.25.7
entries.when: Gaius about AD 200; Eusebius about AD 325

entries.title: Eusebius, Church History 2.22.2 and 2.25.5
entries.text: Eusebius writes that “it is said” Paul was released, preached again, and suffered martyrdom when he came to Rome a second time, and that “Paul was beheaded in Rome itself” under Nero.

cols.label: Acts 22: Paul to the crowd in Jerusalem

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Brought up and taught here; arrested here.

places.name: Damascus

places.name: Arabia
places.note: Where he went after his calling.

places.name: Antioch in Syria
places.note: The church that sent him out.

places.name: Lystra
places.note: Stoned here. Where Paul found Timothy (Acts 16:1).

places.name: Troas
places.note: The vision of the man of Macedonia.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Two years in his own hired house.

places.name: Illyricum
places.note: The limit of his preaching when he wrote Romans.

places.name: Spain
places.note: Planned (Romans 15:24); that he went is tradition (1 Clement 5; the Muratorian fragment).

claim.text: Sent to lay his hands on Saul, who then received his sight and was baptized.
Brought him to the apostles and to Antioch; partner on the first journey; they parted over Mark.
Partner on the second journey; imprisoned with him at Philippi.
Joined him at Lystra and named with him in several letters.
“Luke, the beloved physician”; “Only Luke is with me”.
Left the first journey at Perga; later with Paul again, and “profitable to me for the ministry”.
Went up to Jerusalem with him; left in Crete.
A tentmaker like Paul, with whom he lodged and worked at Corinth.
Aquila's wife; they sailed with Paul as far as Ephesus.
A travelling companion, seized at Ephesus, with him on the voyage, and his “fellowprisoner”.
Travelled with him and carried his letters.
Travelled with him; left sick at Miletum.
Brought the Philippians' gift to Paul in prison.
A fellowlabourer of whom Paul later writes, “Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world”.

scripture.text: Acts ends with Paul two whole years in his own hired house in Rome, “Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.”

In 2 Timothy he writes as a prisoner in Rome who has already made his “first answer” in court: “the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith”.
Whether Paul wrote 2 Timothy is debated, as the Letters page shows; Scripture does not record his death.

tradition.text: Clement of Rome writes that Paul had been “seven times in bonds”, had “preached in the East and in the West”, reached “the farthest bounds of the West”, and when he had borne his testimony before the rulers “departed from the world”.
Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, writes that Peter and Paul taught in Italy and “suffered martyrdom at the same time”.

Gaius, a Roman churchman, points to the apostles' “trophies” at the Vatican and on the Ostian Way.

items.q: Did the men with Saul hear the voice? Acts 9:7 says they were “hearing a voice”; Acts 22:9 that “they heard not the voice of him that spake to me”.
items.full: Did the men with Saul hear the voice? Acts 9:7 says they were “hearing a voice”; Acts 22:9 that “they heard not the voice of him that spake to me”. (In date order.)
items.from: This page

views.label: They heard a sound, not the words
views.holders: Matthew Henry (early 18th century); W. J. Conybeare and J. S. Howson (1891), who also report Wordsworth and Hackett

argument.text: Henry: they heard “a confused noise” but did not understand what was said. Conybeare and Howson: the voice spoke articulately to Saul, but to the rest it was “a sound mysterious and indistinct”.

views.label: Leave the differences as they stand
views.holders: W. J. Conybeare and J. S. Howson (1891)

argument.text: They judge it “both more prudent and more honest to leave these well-known discrepancies exactly as they are found in the Bible”, and note that readers explain them differently according to their view of inspiration.

items.q: Was Paul released after Acts 28 and imprisoned again?
items.full: Was Paul released after Acts 28 and imprisoned again? (Most widely held view in these sources first.)
items.from: This page

views.label: Released, travelled, re-arrested, executed
views.holders: Eusebius (about AD 325); Conybeare and Howson (1891); Schaff (1890), who is “disposed to admit” it; Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Clement's “farthest bounds of the West”, the Muratorian fragment's journey to Spain, Paul's own plan to visit Spain, and the journeys in the letters to Timothy and Titus that Acts has no room for.

views.label: No release: he died at the end of the Roman custody
views.holders: Wieseler and Schrader, as reported and answered by Conybeare and Howson (1891)

argument.text: Acts and the other early sources are silent about later travel, and “the farthest bounds of the West” may mean Rome itself.

views.label: The letters to Timothy and Titus are not Paul's, so they prove nothing either way
views.holders: F. C. Baur and others, as reported by Schaff (1890) and Rutherfurd (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: On this view the journeys those letters mention are no evidence for a release.

items.q: When did these things happen? Scripture gives no years; two public-domain reckonings, side by side.
items.full: When did these things happen? Scripture gives no years; two public-domain reckonings, side by side. (Older first.)
items.from: This page

views.label: Ramsay (1895)
views.holders: W. M. Ramsay, St. Paul the Traveller, Chronological Index

argument.text: Conversion AD 33; first journey from spring 47 to August 49; council winter 49-50; arrival in Jerusalem at Pentecost 57; Rome to the end of 61; second trial 67.

views.label: Robertson (1915)
views.holders: A. T. Robertson, ISBE, “Paul, the Apostle”, part 3

argument.text: Stephen's death, and so the conversion, about 35; first journey 47-48 (or 48-49); council 49 (or 50); arrest spring 57; reaches Rome early in 60; released 63 or early 64; death by early summer 68, possibly 67. Robertson warns: “There is not a single date in the life of Paul that is beyond dispute, though several are narrowed to a fine point.”

items.q: Saul and Paul: one man?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: Saul and Paul are one man: “Saul, (who also is called Paul,)”.

items.q: When does Saul become Paul?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: The narrative of Acts calls him Saul up to Acts 13:9 and Paul from then on; his letters use only Paul.

items.q: An apostle, but not of the Twelve?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: He calls himself an apostle “not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ”, and “the least of the apostles”; Acts calls Barnabas and Paul “the apostles”.

items.q: How did his story end?
items.from: How the story ends: Scripture beside tradition, never blended

argument.text: Acts ends with Paul two whole years in his own hired house in Rome, “Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.”

In 2 Timothy he writes as a prisoner in Rome who has already made his “first answer” in court: “the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith”.
Whether Paul wrote 2 Timothy is debated, as the Letters page shows; Scripture does not record his death.

items.q: Did Paul write Ephesians, Colossians and the pastoral letters?
items.full: Did Paul write Ephesians, Colossians and the pastoral letters?
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: All by Paul
views.holders: The ancient church (Eusebius: Paul's letters "well known and undisputed"); for Ephesians and Colossians Bleek, Meyer, B. Weiss, Alford and Farrar; for the pastoral letters Huther, Wiesinger, Wieseler, Lange, Alford, Farrar, Salmon, B. Weiss and others (as listed by Schaff and ISBE)

argument.text: Each letter names Paul in its first verse, and ancient writers accepted all of them. Marcion did reject the pastoral letters, which, Tertullian notes, "all treat of ecclesiastical discipline". Schaff answers the vocabulary argument by noting that Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians and Philippians also have many words found nowhere else in the New Testament.

views.label: Ephesians or Colossians not by Paul
views.holders: De Wette (Ephesians "a verbose expansion" of Colossians); Renan and Ewald (kept Colossians, gave up Ephesians); Mayerhoff (Colossians an abridgment of Ephesians); Baur, Schwegler and Hilgenfeld (both, from a later anti-Gnostic writer); Holtzmann, Pfleiderer and others

argument.text: The two letters overlap so closely that critics have argued one is a later writer's reworking of the other, or both of something earlier. ISBE concludes instead for "simultaneous authorship by one writer".

views.label: The pastoral letters not by Paul
views.holders: J. E. C. Schmidt and Schleiermacher (1 Timothy); Baur, who dated them about 150; Holtzmann, whose 1880 work made the fullest case from their vocabulary; Renan, Pfleiderer, Ewald, Hausrath and others

argument.text: Holtzmann made the fullest case from their language: Schaff, citing him, counts 169 of their words found nowhere else in the New Testament. Baur dated them about 150, and Pfleiderer placed 2 Timothy under Trajan and the other two under Hadrian. Renan thought a forger had worked in a few genuine notes of Paul's.

items.q: Was Paul released after the two years in Rome, and imprisoned a second time?
items.full: Was Paul released after the two years in Rome, and imprisoned a second time?
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: Released, travelled, arrested again and executed
views.holders: Eusebius; Conybeare and Howson, adding Chrysostom and Jerome; ISBE; Easton; Schaff ("disposed to admit" it)

argument.text: The pastoral letters mention journeys that do not fit Acts: Timothy left at Ephesus, Titus in Crete, a winter at Nicopolis, a cloak at Troas. Clement of Rome says Paul reached "the farthest bounds of the West"; the Muratorian fragment speaks of a journey from Rome to Spain; and Eusebius reports that Paul was sent out again to preach and martyred on a second visit to Rome, citing 2 Timothy's "first answer".

views.label: Not released
views.holders: Wieseler and Schrader (as criticised by Conybeare and Howson)

argument.text: Acts and the other early sources are silent about later travel, and Clement's "extremity of the West" (Conybeare and Howson's rendering) may simply mean Rome: Wieseler translated the words as the sovereign of Rome, and Schrader argued they cannot mean Spain because Paul was not martyred there.

views.label: Pastoral letters written during the Acts period
views.holders: One proposal reported by Schaff

argument.text: The journeys could be unrecorded trips during Paul's three years at Ephesus, about 56-57.

views.label: No evidence either way
views.holders: Those who deny that Paul wrote the pastoral letters

argument.text: If the pastoral letters are not Paul's, their travel notes say nothing about his last years.

items.q: Where was Paul held when he wrote the prison letters: Rome, Caesarea or Ephesus?
items.full: Where was Paul held when he wrote the prison letters: Rome, Caesarea or Ephesus?
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: Rome
views.holders: The oldest tradition and "most modern writers" (Lightfoot); Conybeare and Howson; the ISBE articles; Easton

argument.text: Acts ends with two years in Rome, in a rented house under guard, receiving all who came. Greetings from "Caesar's household" fit Rome; Lightfoot held they could not fairly fit Caesarea, and that at Caesarea, having appealed to Caesar, Paul had no reason to expect release and a visit to Macedonia.

views.label: Caesarea
views.holders: Böttger, Thiersch, Reuss and H. A. W. Meyer for Ephesians, Colossians and Philemon; H. E. G. Paulus, Böttger and Thiersch for Philippians (reported by Lightfoot)

argument.text: Paul was also held two years at Caesarea under Felix, with friends free to visit, and the "palace" of Philippians 1:13 is the same Greek word used for Herod's judgment hall there.

views.label: Ephesus
views.holders: The Latin prologue to Colossians in Codex Fuldensis; Deissmann, Lisco, Albertz and Bacon, "a growing opinion" in 1915 (as reported by Robertson, ISBE)

argument.text: Paul's own record mentions prisons "more frequent" than Acts reports, a fight with beasts at Ephesus and deadly trouble in Asia, and Clement of Rome says he was in bonds seven times.

items.q: Did Paul write 2 Thessalonians, and which of the two letters came first?
items.full: Did Paul write 2 Thessalonians, and which of the two letters came first?
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: Not by Paul
views.holders: Baur (who, Schaff reports, regarded the first letter as an imitation of the second); Hilgenfeld, who dated it to Trajan's reign as "a sort of Pauline Apocalypse" (reported by Schaff)

argument.text: Its teaching on the Lord's coming seems to differ from the first letter ("In the First Letter he coaxes; in the Second Letter he commands", as Walker summarises the case), its tone is cooler, and its "man of sin" is unlike anything else in Paul.

views.label: By Paul
views.holders: Walker (ISBE); Harnack, who thought it was addressed to a Jewish-Christian group in the church

argument.text: Jesus' own teaching, Walker notes, holds together the call to "watch, for in such an hour as they think not the Son of man cometh" and the warning that "the end is not yet"; and a sterner second note is natural if the gentler first one had not worked. Walker saw scholars of every camp returning to the traditional view.

views.label: Written before 1 Thessalonians
views.holders: Grotius and Ewald, who held both letters genuine (reported by Schaff)

argument.text: The order of the two letters in the Bible is not necessarily the order in which they were written.

items.q: How many letters did Paul write to Corinth, and which was the letter written "with many tears"?
items.full: How many letters did Paul write to Corinth, and which was the letter written "with many tears"?
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: Four letters, two of them lost
views.holders: Read from the letters themselves

argument.text: The two surviving letters point to at least four: a lost earlier letter about not keeping company with fornicators, 1 Corinthians, a letter written "out of much affliction and anguish of heart", and 2 Corinthians. Shaw (ISBE) suggests that 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 may preserve a stray piece of the lost first letter.

views.label: The tearful letter is 1 Corinthians
views.holders: Easton

argument.text: Easton applies Paul's description of anguish and tears to 1 Corinthians itself. He also doubts any unrecorded painful visit, reading "the third time I am ready to come" as an intention only.

views.label: A separate letter, now lost
views.holders: Shaw (ISBE)

argument.text: Shaw treats "the severe letter" as a letter of its own, written after a painful second visit that Acts does not record.

views.label: The tearful letter survives as 2 Corinthians 10-13
views.holders: Hausrath (1870), followed by Schmiedel, Pfleiderer, Lipsius, Clemen, von Soden, McGiffert, Plummer, Moffatt, Peake, J. H. Kennedy and others (as listed by Shaw, ISBE)

argument.text: Everyone agrees on a remarkable change of tone at chapter 10. On this view the last four chapters are part of the painful letter, later joined to the gentler one.

views.label: 2 Corinthians is one letter
views.holders: Sanday, A. Robertson, Holtzmann, Beyschlag, Weizsäcker, Sabatier, Godet, Bernard, Denney, Weiss and Zahn (as listed by Shaw, ISBE)

argument.text: The change of tone is real, but it does not prove that two letters were joined; A. Robertson called the case "decidedly not proven".

items.q: Was the last chapter of Romans, with its long list of greetings, written to Rome?
items.full: Was the last chapter of Romans, with its long list of greetings, written to Rome?
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: A note to Ephesus attached later
views.holders: Reuss, Ewald and Farrar (named by Schaff); others reported by Moule (ISBE)

argument.text: Paul greets so many people in a city he had never visited that some thought the greetings, Romans 16:1-15 or 16:3-20, belonged to a separate note sent to Ephesus.

views.label: One circular letter with several endings
views.holders: Renan

argument.text: Renan guessed that an editor had combined four copies of a single circular letter, each with a different ending.

views.label: Chapters 15-16 not genuine
views.holders: Baur

argument.text: Baur rejected the last two chapters altogether; Hilgenfeld and Pfleiderer defended them against him.

views.label: Part of the letter to Rome
views.holders: Hort, A. Robertson, Hilgenfeld, Pfleiderer (reported by Moule and Schaff)

argument.text: Of some 300 manuscripts of Romans, Moule reports, not one that is undamaged lacks the complete letter. The doubts in the manuscripts concern the closing doxology, which some copies place after chapter 14 and three, with Marcion, leave out.

items.q: Was "Ephesians" written to Ephesus? The words "at Ephesus" are missing from the oldest manuscripts.
items.full: Was "Ephesians" written to Ephesus? The words "at Ephesus" are missing from the oldest manuscripts.
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: To Ephesus
views.holders: Tertullian, appealing to "the true tradition of the Church"

argument.text: The Textus Receptus and the KJV read "at Ephesus", and the church received the letter under that title.

views.label: To Laodicea
views.holders: Marcion

argument.text: Marcion's collection called it the letter "to the Laodiceans".

views.label: A circular letter for the churches of Asia
views.holders: Archbishop Ussher, who first proposed it; Lightfoot, Conybeare and Howson, Lewis (ISBE), Easton

argument.text: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus lack "at Ephesus"; Origen knew nothing of the words and Basil reported old copies without them. The letter has no personal greetings, though Paul spent three years at Ephesus, and speaks as if some readers had only heard of him. On this view the copy that reached Laodicea is "the epistle from Laodicea" of Colossians 4:16.

items.q: Who were "the churches of Galatia": the old Celtic territory in the north, or the southern cities of the Roman province?
items.full: Who were "the churches of Galatia": the old Celtic territory in the north, or the southern cities of the Roman province?
items.from: Asked on the Paul's letters page

views.label: North Galatia
views.holders: Earlier scholars up to Lightfoot and Salmon; later Chase, Dods, Sabatier, Harnack, H. Holtzmann, Jülicher, Lipsius, Mommsen, Schmiedel, Schürer and others; Findlay himself (as listed by Findlay, ISBE)

argument.text: The letter went to churches in old Galatia around Ancyra, Pessinus and Tavium, which Paul first reached on his second journey when he passed through "the region of Galatia". On this view the letter is later rather than earlier. Robertson judged in 1915 that it "still has the weight of authority".

views.label: South Galatia
views.holders: First proposed by Mynster (1825); then Perrot, Renan, Pfleiderer, Weizsäcker, Ramsay, von Soden, Bartlet, Gifford, Rendall, Sanday ("with hesitation") and others (as listed by Findlay, ISBE)

argument.text: The letter went to Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, the churches Paul founded on his first journey, all inside the Roman province of Galatia. Ramsay's books made this view widely known from 1895, and some of its supporters make Galatians the earliest of Paul's letters.

items.q: Who wrote Hebrews?
items.from: Asked on the Hebrews page

views.label: Paul
views.holders: Pantaenus and Clement of Alexandria (late 2nd century); the Eastern churches; Athanasius (367); later the Latin West through Jerome and Augustine and the councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (419); in modern times Ebrard, Hofmann, Biesenthal, Kay and Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897).

argument.text: For: Timothy is mentioned (13:23), and Origen judged the thoughts to be the apostle's. Pantaenus explained the missing name: Paul, sent to the Gentiles, would not call himself apostle to the Hebrews. Clement added that Paul did not want to put off readers who distrusted him. The KJV's "me in my bonds" (10:34) seemed to point to Paul the prisoner, though Westcott's Greek text reads "the prisoners". Against: Paul says he received his gospel from no man, but this writer learned it from others (2:3), a point Westcott calls grave, even fatal. Origen found the Greek purer than Paul's, the writer always quotes the Greek Old Testament, and the church at Rome long disputed the claim.

views.label: Barnabas
views.holders: Tertullian (about AD 220); revived by Cameron in the 17th century; later Ritschl, Weiss, Renan, Salmon, Grau and Zahn (as listed by Dods and Westcott).

argument.text: For: it is the only named tradition besides Paul. Barnabas was a Levite, which would suit a writer so absorbed in priesthood. His nickname, "son of consolation", uses the same Greek word as the writer's "word of exhortation" (13:22). He was a Greek-speaking Cypriot in Paul's circle. Against: the tradition is found only in North Africa, and Origen does not know it. Dods and Rees treat the word match as coincidence. Davidson thinks his early story hardly fits 2:3.

views.label: Luke
views.holders: Clement of Alexandria (as translator of a letter Paul wrote in Hebrew); reported by Origen; Calvin (Luke or Clement); Delitzsch.

argument.text: For: ancient readers noticed that the style is like that of Acts, a likeness Westcott calls remarkable. Against: it may only mean the writer knew Luke's work or circle. If the letter was never translated from Hebrew, the main reason for naming Luke largely falls away. The Alexandrian cast of the letter's thought is not found in Luke.

views.label: Clement of Rome
views.holders: Reported by Origen; Eusebius (as the likelier translator); mentioned by Calvin.

argument.text: For: Clement's letter to Corinth (about AD 96) borrows heavily from Hebrews; its chapter 36 reworks Heb 1:3–4 and the psalms of 1:5–13. Jerome also noticed the likeness. Against: Westcott reads the parallels as Clement using Hebrews, just as he uses Paul's letters. Clement combines but does not create, and the depth of thought is far apart.

views.label: Apollos
views.holders: First suggested by Martin Luther (as reported by Westcott and Dods); then Bleek, Tholuck, Hilgenfeld, Lünemann, Reuss, Pfleiderer, Alford, Farrar, Plumptre and Kurtz; Bartlet in the 1911 Britannica, writing to Asia.

argument.text: For: Acts describes him as an Alexandrian Jew, "an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures", who showed from the scriptures that Jesus was the Christ. He belonged to Paul's circle. Davidson felt no better words could describe the writer of Hebrews. Against: no ancient writer suggests him. Westcott notes there is no evidence that Apollos wrote anything, and sees the guess as a reluctance to admit we do not know.

views.label: Priscilla (and Aquila)
views.holders: Adolf Harnack (1900, as reported by Dods and Rees); Bleek had almost argued for Aquila; Rendel Harris was sympathetic.

argument.text: For: the couple taught Apollos, worked with Paul, knew Timothy and hosted a church in their home at Rome. Harnack read the change between "I" and "we" as a sign of two writers, and argued that the name was dropped because of prejudice against a woman teaching. Against: the writer speaks of himself as one man (11:32; 13:19, 22–23) and seems to be one of the leaders, as Dods points out; Rees answers Harnack that Paul too moves between "I" and "we", in Romans for one, where no one suggests two writers.

views.label: Silas (Silvanus)
views.holders: Named as possible by Westcott; listed by Easton and in the ISBE.

argument.text: For: Silas belonged to Paul's circle, and 1 Peter was written "by Silvanus". Against: Westcott says only that the idea is consistent with what we know of him.

views.label: Others
views.holders: Mark (E. S. Lowndes, as reported by Westcott); Philip the deacon and Aristion (listed in the ISBE).

argument.text: Mostly guesswork. Rees calls these names little more than names to us. Jesus' own disciples are ruled out, because the writer heard the gospel second-hand (2:3).

views.label: Unknown
views.holders: Origen; Dods (1910), who thought it best to confess our ignorance; Rees in the ISBE (1915).

argument.text: Origen said that only God knows who wrote the letter. Dods preferred to admit ignorance, though he thought Aquila fitted a Roman destination as well as anyone. Rees leaned toward someone like Apollos but left the answer with God.

items.q: Which letter was written first?
items.from: Asked on the The letters of the New Testament page

views.label: James
views.holders: Philip Schaff (1890); J. B. Mayor (1892) dated it to the 40s

argument.text: Schaff placed James "before A.D. 50" and called it "probably the oldest of the New Testament books"; it "takes no notice of the circumcision controversy" that fills Galatians.

views.label: Galatians
views.holders: John Calvin (1548); some holders of the South Galatian view (reported by Robertson, ISBE)

argument.text: Calvin thought Galatians was written "before that consultation had been held" in Acts 15, since Paul would surely have cited the council's decree; Robertson reports that some South Galatian scholars make it "the very earliest of Paul's Epistles".

views.label: 1 Thessalonians
views.holders: M. G. Easton (1897); George Milligan (1908, reported by Robertson, ISBE)

argument.text: Written from Corinth soon after Timothy returned from Thessalonica: "the first of all Paul's epistles" (Easton).

items.q: Which visit to Jerusalem took Titus with Paul (Galatians 2:1)?
items.full: Which visit to Jerusalem took Titus with Paul (Galatians 2:1)? (Older view first.)
items.from: Asked on Titus’s page

views.label: The council of Acts 15
views.holders: Irenaeus (about 180); Lightfoot (1890); Smith (1884); Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Lightfoot: the visit “has from the earliest times been identified with the visit recorded in Acts xv”: the same places, people and question. Rutherfurd counts Titus among “certain other of them” in Acts 15:2.

views.label: The famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30
views.holders: Ramsay (1895)

argument.text: Ramsay takes Titus to have been an assistant on the relief journey, and argues Paul would not have brought “an uncircumcised Greek” to the council itself.

items.q: Was Titus circumcised at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:3–5)?
items.full: Was Titus circumcised at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:3–5)? (Most widely held view first.)
items.from: Asked on Titus’s page

views.label: No: Paul did not yield
views.holders: Lightfoot (1890), with “the vast majority of early writers”; Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Lightfoot: the incident is told to show Paul never conceded circumcision, and Paul “could scarcely say ‘we yielded no not for an hour’ in the same breath” as confessing it.

views.label: Yes: he was circumcised, but not by compulsion
views.holders: Farrar (1879); Pelagius, the one early exception Lightfoot found; “several modern critics” (Lightfoot)

argument.text: Farrar asks why Paul's sentence is “so ambiguous, so involved” if he did not yield, and reads “was compelled” to mean Titus was circumcised “but not under compulsion”.

items.q: Who made the vow at Cenchrea (Acts 18:18)?
items.full: Who made the vow at Cenchrea (Acts 18:18)? (Order: as in these sources.)
items.from: Asked on Priscilla and Aquila’s page

views.label: Aquila
views.holders: Conybeare and Howson (1891), in their text, “left as it stood in the earlier editions”

argument.text: They describe Aquila ending a Jewish vow before sailing; their own note admits that “the arguments from the structure of the original are rather in favour of referring the vow, not to Aquila, but to St. Paul”.

views.label: Paul
views.holders: Ramsay (1895)

argument.text: Ramsay: “Though the grammatical construction of v. 18 would suggest that Aquila made the vow … the natural emphasis marks Paul as the subject here.”

items.q: Why did John Mark turn back at Perga?
items.full: Why did John Mark turn back at Perga? (Scripture does not say; views in the order they were published.)
items.from: Asked on John Mark’s page

views.label: He did not like the work, or wanted to see his mother
views.holders: Matthew Henry (1706-1721)

argument.text: Henry offers both reasons as guesses and adds that Mark left “without the consent of Paul and Barnabas”.

views.label: No reason can be known
views.holders: Smith (1884: “for some unexplained reason”); Fenlon (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907: Luke “does not state”)

argument.text: Acts gives only Paul's later complaint that Mark “went not with them to the work”.

views.label: He shrank from the toil
views.holders: MacRory (1910), who says Acts 15:38 “seems to suggest that he feared the toil”

argument.text: The journey after Perga led inland to Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium and Lystra.

views.label: He objected to offering salvation to Gentiles on faith alone
views.holders: J. H. Farmer (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Farmer points to the conversion of Sergius Paulus at Paphos just before, where Paul takes the lead, and to Paul's strong words in Acts 15:38.

items.q: Scripture does not record Paul's death. Acts names no emperor at his appeal, only “Caesar” (Acts 25:11); the KJV's note after 2 Timothy that names Nero is not Scripture.
items.from: What Scripture does not say

items.q: Scripture does not say whether Paul ever reached Spain.
items.from: What Scripture does not say

items.q: Scripture does not say whether Paul was ever married; when he wrote 1 Corinthians he was unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7-8).
items.from: What Scripture does not say

items.q: Scripture does not describe his appearance, and does not say what his “thorn in the flesh” was (2 Corinthians 12:7).
items.from: What Scripture does not say

notSaid: Scripture does not record Paul's death. Acts names no emperor at his appeal, only “Caesar” (Acts 25:11); the KJV's note after 2 Timothy that names Nero is not Scripture.
Scripture does not say whether Paul ever reached Spain.
Scripture does not say whether Paul was ever married; when he wrote 1 Corinthians he was unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7-8).
Scripture does not describe his appearance, and does not say what his “thorn in the flesh” was (2 Corinthians 12:7).
